Title: Partner conflict during their index pregnancy and its correlates among a cohort of six weeks postpartum women in Ethiopia
Text:
Partner conflict during their index 
pregnancy and its correlates among 
a cohort of six weeks postpartum 
women in Ethiopia
Solomon Abrha Damtew
1, Niguse Tadele Atnafu2, Mahari Yihdego Gidey3, 
Tesfamichael Awoke Sisay3 & Metages Yohannes4
Current intimate partner violence (IPV) during pregnancy was found to be associated with adverse 
health outcomes including pregnancy loss, preterm labor, pregnancy complications, hypertension, 
delivering low birth weight baby, physical injuries and stress. IPV in Ethiopia is considerably high. This 
study aimed at determining the prevalence of the IPV during the index pregnancy as measured at 
six weeks postpartum among women in their extended six weeks postpartum period and identify its 
correlates. Documenting the magnitude of IPV during the index pregnancy as measured six weeks in 
the postpartum period and identifying factors affecting it could be imperative to generate actionable 
evidence. Generating such an evidence contributed its share for the Health Minister and other relevant 
partners in tracking progress towards achievement of the sustainable development goals (SDGs) 
5.2.1 by 2030. This study used Performance Monitoring for Action Ethiopian (PMA_ET) merged cohort 
one baseline and six weeks postpartum data which had enrolled and collected data from currently 
pregnant women. Frequencies were computed to describe the study participant’s characteristics, and 
chi-square statistics was calculated to assess cell sample size adequacy. Multilevel binary logistics 
regression statistical modeling was employed to identify correlates of IPV. Results were presented in 
the form percentages and odds ratio with 95% Confidence Intervals. Candidate variables were selected 
using p-value of 0.25. Statistical significance was declared at p-value of 0.05. The overall proportion 
of IPV during the index pregnancy as measured six weeks postpartum was 12.14% (95%CI: 10.66%, 
13.79%). A slightly higher percentage of women reported that they have experienced at least one 
form of sexual IPV 8.09% (95% CI: 6.91%, 9.44%) than experiencing at least one form of physical IPV 
6.02% (95% CI: 4.94%, 7.31%). After controlling confounders, the likelihood of experiencing at least 
one form of physical and/or sexual IPV was 2.14 (95%CI: 1.04, 4.38) times higher among women whose 
husband had other wives’ compared to those who did not have. Women who were residents of Afar 
region had only 0.14 (95%CI: 0.03, 0.79) odds of experiencing one form of physical and/or sexual IPV. 
The overall experience of at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV was found to be 12.14%. A 
statistically non-significant slightly higher percentage of women reported that they have experienced 
at least one form of sexual IPV than experiencing at least one form of physical IPV. Activities and 
efforts which are specific to regions are needed to address the problem of polygamy are hoped to 
address the problem IPV during pregnancy. Such activities should be tailored along with the maternal 
and new born care continuum. Further implication of this study is installing violence and contraceptive 
related preconception care packages in the health system which is imperative in the combat against 
IPV and any form of gender based violence. In addition, creating institutional capacity in the health 
system through strengthening and expanding one stop centers to provide medical treatment, 
care, and psychosocial support along with support for victims and survivors can be considered as 
imperative. Moreover, the finding gave an insight that installing rapid referral system and linkage to 
the legal system is key. Similarly, working on early marriage and counseling on childbirth; and spaced 
pregnancies for those young couples is implied on. Most importantly, determining the prevalence of 
violence could serve as one of the indicators to monitor the progress towards SDG 5.2.1 and to look for 
any strategy and policy changes needed in light of the observed progress.
Keywords  Partner Conflict Intimate Partner violence, Physical intimate Partner violence, Sexual intimate 
Violence, Women Health, Ethiopia, PMA_ET, Extended Postpartum Period

The World Health Organization (WHO) defined intimate partner Violence (IPV) as a self-reported experience 
of one or more acts of physical aggression and/or sexual violence which has been being committed and had been 
committed by a current or a former partner since the age of 15 years1. IPV is one aspect of gender-based violence 
and/or domestic violence. It has one of the three forms: physical, sexual and emotional abuse and/or violence 
that has been committed by a current and/or former intimate partner1–4. IPV can be current, happened in the 
past one year, or a prior one that happened before one year1–3,5–7. This study, however, focused on measuring 
women experience of at least on form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index pregnancy as measured 
in the extended six weeks postpartum period among women who were enrolled during their pregnancy and 
followed one year post-partum.
Evidences revealed that IPV has been found more prevalent in low- and middle-income countries, although 
it is common in both developing and developed countries2,3,5–7. In Africa, the prevalence of IPV ranged from 2 
to 57%, with an average overall prevalence of 15.23%5,8–10. In Ethiopia, one in three women of reproductive age 
group experienced at least one form of physical and/or sexual violence2,11; and nearly half of women experience 
IPV during pregnancy in North West Ethiopia12. IPV in Ethiopia ranged from 12% in Yirgalem13 to 44.7% Abay 
Chome district14, with an average prevalence of 26.1% nationally15. A recent similar study16 reported that 16.7% 
pregnant women have reported experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV thus far in their 
index pregnancy.
A multifaceted factors has been contributing for this higher burden of IPV and the associate sequela and 
toll. Cultural and social acceptance of violence coupled with a male-dominant society exacerbated the impact 
of IPV during pregnancy and hampers prevention and control efforts as well17–19. Women and husband 
sociodemographic factors15,20,21, parity, cohabitation duration, and other reproductive health (RH) characteristics 
were found to affect IPV during the index pregnancy22 as measured among postpartum women8,21,23. However, 
these studies are limited in geographic area, based on cross sectional data and; did not address all possible 
confounders; and studied women who delivered in past 2 year or more along with pregnant women by the time 
of the survey. While this study used merged baseline and six weeks postpartum data from a longitudinal study 
which asked currently pregnant women who were at various months of gestation during the survey whether they 
experienced any of the 10 physical and/or sexual IPV items during their index pregnancy. In addition, this study 
attempted to control available integral and possibly derived enumeration area level variables. There was one 
similar study16 on secondary data analysis of the 2021 Performance and monitoring for action Ethiopia baseline 
survey though it was not nationally representative since the survey did not collected data from Tigray Region 
due to the conflict erupted16,24,25.
Moreover, IPV during pregnancy is found to be associated with adverse health outcomes15,20,26–29 including 
pregnancy loss, preterm labor, pregnancy complications, hypertension, delivering low birth weight baby, physical 
injuries and stress8,22,27,30–33. Evidences have showed that IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in 
extended six weeks postpartum period has more prominent health effect on the mother and adverse pregnancy 
outcomes22,28,29,31,32. Violence has an impact on the health of women apart from its economic and social impact. 
The impact is more pronounced when it is committed in the postpartum period and during pregnancy3,8,26,34. It 
has also psycho-social impact on the victim women including depressive symptoms and trauma24,35–37.
To address such an important public health problem, minimize its health effect, associated toll and; to intervene 
on amenable factors contributing towards it, violence against women has received an international attention as 
of 2016 in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with target 5.2.1. This goal claimed elimination of all 
forms violence against women and girls in public and private spheres, which calls up on gender equality and 
empowerment of women and girls38,39. This global attention has been extended to end abuse, exploitation, and 
trafficking and any forms violence against children in target 16.2 under the SDG goal 161,3, and21. In response 
to this international attention on reproductive health (RH) indicators in general and IPV in particular, the 
Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia Health Ministry (FEDRE_MOH) has adapted all RH and IPV related 
SDG goals and targets. All RH-related SDG goals were included in the new national RH policy running from 
2021 to 2025. In addition, a directorate was established in the ministry and IPV focal person was assigned in 
region, zone, and woreda level health offices. Furthermore, large hospitals have opened one-stop centers for IPV 
survivor treatment, care, support, and linkage to the legal body as part of the national strategy2.
Being short of half way in the SDG era, the aim of this study was to measure the magnitude of IPV during 
the index pregnancy and identify individual and enumeration area level factors affecting it by using nationally 
representative community based data from PMA Ethiopia. In addition, determining the prevalence of violence is 
one of the proposed indicators to monitor the progress in SDG 5.2.1: elimination of all forms of violence, which 
is achieved by such national level evidence generation3.The findings could be used as an input to monitor the 
achievement of target 5.2.13,39. Hence, the finding of this study help the ministry and other relevant partners in 
tracking achievement of the elimination of all forms of violence against women and girls by 20302,3,39.
Methods and data sources
Design, population and study sample
Performance Monitoring for action (PMA) collected national level representative cross sectional and longitudinal 
data on key maternal, new born health and index pregnancy care indicators along with family planning, women 
empowerment/norms and other relevant reproductive health national priority indicators.

Performance Monitoring for Action (PMA) employed a two stage cluster sampling; in the first stage 
enumeration areas (EA) were selected. In each selected EAs census was conducted to screen and enroll pregnant 
women and less than 6 weeks postpartum women. This study used community based baseline data along with 
the six weeks postpartum data from a prospective cohort study with 6 weeks, 6 months and one year postpartum 
follow up interviews. These data were collected from pregnant and postpartum women in Ethiopia from six 
regions: namely: Addis Ababa, Afar, Amhara, Oromia, SNNPR and Tigray. The survey has been started by 
recruiting and enrolling pregnant women and puerperal women less than six weeks which was followed by 
administering the female baseline questionnaire. Then these panel of women were followed and interviewed at 
their 6 weeks, 6 months and one year postpartum as follow up interviews. However, this study further analyzed 
and presented data sets from the baseline and six weeks postpartum follow up interview survey.
Nationally representative baseline and six weeks postpartum follow up data collected from pregnant and 
postpartum women were further analyzed in this study. After the complete census was conducted in the selected 
enumeration areas all pregnant women with gestational age of 1 to 9 months who were either usual residents in 
the selected EAs or who came to the EA to give birth were enrolled and followed one year post postpartum. This 
analysis was restricted to a total of 2,304 pregnant women who were married or living together with a partner 
and completed the baseline and the six weeks follow up postpartum interviews with complete responses for the 
ten physical and/or sexual IPV measurement items. The overall sample size and cell sample size adequacy was 
checked and found adequate to generating unbiased estimates for the outcome variable, IPV.
A two-stage stratified cluster sampling method was used to select enumeration areas. In order not to miss all 
pregnant and six week postpartum women by then complete census was conducted in the selected enumeration 
areas. The main sampling units or enumeration areas (EAs) were chosen using the frame from Ethiopia Population 
and Housing Census (PHC), which was performed in 2019 by the Ethiopia Central Statistical Services. Of the 
total of 265 EAs which were chosen in the first stage with independent selection in each sampling stratum and 
a probability proportional to EA size; data from pregnant women and six weeks follow up survey which were 
collected from 217 EAs selected from the six panel regions were included in this further analysis. In second 
stage, a census of all households was conducted in all the selected EAs to obtain adequate sample size of pregnant 
women and to improve the study´s power. The protocol of PMA Ethiopia contains all the details on sample 
design and selection probabilities, design effects and sampling methods40.
In order to maximize the sample of pregnant women; a census of all the panel enumeration areas (EAs) 
was conducted. All women aged 15–49 who were usual members of the household were screened by using 
self-reported current pregnancy status and approximate gestational age. If pregnant, they were approached for 
enrollment in the panel and voluntarily consented women were recruited to participate the study. For the census, 
a 95% response rate was assumed, that the average number of women aged 15–49 per household is 0.98, and 
of these, 10% have reported of being pregnant or 42 days postpartum– the calculated sample size was found 
sufficient to examine selected key maternal and newborn health (MNH) indicators at the national level with 5% 
margin of error.
The fieldwork was executed by Addis Ababa University’s School of Public Health in a collaborative efforts 
with the Ethiopian Public Health Association, the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia Health Minister, 
Central Statistical Services, Bill & Melinda Gates Institute for Population and Reproductive Health (Johns 
Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health)40.
Variables
Outcome variable
IPV among pregnant was measured by asking a series of 10 yes/no questions (7 measure physical abuse and 3 
sexual abuse) as measured in the extended six weeks postpartum period. If a women responded yes for at least 
of the ten items she is considered as experiencing IPV during their pregnancy and no if otherwise. The ten 
yes/no questions were summed after excluding the do not know and no response, response options. Women 
who reported that they experienced at least one of the ten items at any time during their index pregnancy 
were considered as experiencing at least one form of physical and or sexual intimate partner violence (IPV) 
during their pregnancy while those reported not experiencing any of these ten items during their pregnancy 
were considered as not experiencing IPV21 (Table 1).
Independent variables
Women were asked about their antenatal care sought thus in their pregnancy, partner support and perceived 
community encouragement on the use the three main domains of the maternal and newborn care continuum 
components, their reproductive and sexual history, their birth preparedness and complication readiness, about 
their agreement and disagreement on girls and women empowerment towards contraceptive use and sexual and 
reproductive issues, contraceptive use history and there fertility intention.
Independent variables were classified into individual-level variables and enumeration area-level variables. 
Individual-level independent variables further categorized into socio demographic/economic characteristics 
variables, parity and other RH characteristics, knowledge on contraceptive related characteristics, husband 
socio-demography and support related characteristics.
Group or enumeration area (EA) level variables included two integral variables namely, region and place 
of residence while three derived EA level variables, EA level wealth derived from the household level wealth, 
while proportion of women who completed secondary or above educational level per EA and her husband/
partner who completed the same educational level per EA were derived from the respective women and 
husband/partner educational status. “Region” was grouped into six categories: 1= Tigray, 2= Afar, 3 = Amhara, 
4 = Oromia, 7 = SNNPRs and 10 = Addis Ababa city administration. Place of residence follows the default urban/
rural classification.

Data quality management and control
Data completeness for variables and items for creating composite variables was checked by exploratory data 
analysis following which any item nonresponse was excluded from the analysis. Frequency run to exclude 
responses with do not know (DNK) and no response (NR).
PMA Ethiopia used of standard and pretested tool, intensive training with mock interviews for resident 
enumerators was provided, close supervisor during filed work, timely progress report and correction, 10% 
random check were some of the modalities used to maintain the quality of the collected data, the detail is 
reported somewhere else40.
Analysis and measurement
The panel baseline data set merged with six weeks postpartum data sets were used for this analysis. Stata v16 
was used for this analysis. Frequencies and percentages were computed to characterize the study population. 
Chi-square test statistics was computed to check cell sample size adequacy and the sample size was found to be 
adequate to provide unbiased estimates.
First the data set was kept by female respondent baseline questionnaire, six weeks follow up interview results 
and then by marital status. This was followed by excluding responses from the outcome response categories; 
do not know and no response. This preliminary analysis and data cleaning resulted a final sample size of 2,304.
Exploratory data analysis was run for data cleaning thereby checking item nonresponse rate for every variable 
and don’t know response which were later excluded from the analysis. Following this variable were recoded to 
create biological plausible categories along with checking distribution of the recoded variables using mean and 
proportion.
Derived EA level variables such as proportion of pregnant women or husbands who completed secondary 
education per EA and proportion of women who were residing in the well to do household per EA were 
computed from the respective individual level variable and household level wealth index respectively. Person 
correlation was calculated and found to be 0.87 for the household wealth index and EA level wealth, hence, the 
drive EA level wealth was not included in the final models.
Multilevel binary logistics regression statistical regression modeling was run to identify important predictors 
of encountering at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV among pregnant women. At bivariate analysis 
a p value cut of 0.25 was used to select candidate variable for multilevel multivariate binary logistics regression 
analysis. Results were presented in the form of percentage, and odds ratio with 95% CI. Significance was declared 
at a significance level of 0.05. Results were reported based on weighted count.
Four models were run; the first model is the null model: the null/intercept only model without any predictor 
variables but EA as random intercept, followed by computing intra-cluster correlation coefficient (ICC) for 
the null model. Model II: this model included only individual level variable followed by ICC computation and 
percentage variation change (PVC). Model III: this model included only the five EA level variable followed by ICC 
computation and PVC for the model. Model IV: this was the final model in which both individual and EA level 
variables were accounted followed by ICC computation and along with computing Akaike, Bayesian information 
criteria and log likelihood were used to assess model fitness to identify the best fitted model. Model IV was the 
best fitted model since it has the lower AIC/BIC and higher log likelihood. Moreover, intimate partner violence 
(IPV) is highly culturally embedded and women from the same enumeration area (EA) have commonalities. 
Thus, assuming that each observation is independent while using single level conventional logistics regression 
might not be kept due to the clustering nature of observation which led us to use a multilevel model building 
process to account for the clustering of observations within each EA with regard to IPV41. Furthermore, either 
the use of stratified multistage cluster sampling, or unequal probabilities of selection from source populations 
for study population, due to oversampling of key population subgroups national/from some regions make 
nationally representative data such PMA to have complex data in nature and data structure. Therefore, sampling 
weights were applied during the estimation of proportions and the respective confidence interval to account for 
the sample design and unequal selection probabilities from the source population to the study samples42.

In conclusion, these design related factors, having a nested data structure (women nested in enumeration 
areas) and the very clustering nature the observations by design which was replicated in the random effect 
measure analysis: witnessed by a 41% clustering of IPV cases was explained by the similarity in enumeration 
areas from where women were recruited. These supported the use of multilevel modeling. This 41% is a measure 
of clustering of IPV case due to the similarity in EAs they were recruited and is the called intra cluster correlation 
(ICC) is the ratio of the variation in IPV due to the variation in the enumeration area where women recruited 
and the total variation in IPV cases due the variation in individual woman characteristics and the variation in EA 
from which each women recruited has supported the use of a multilevel regression modeling given the level of 
clustering was found far beyond the threshold for the independent observation assumption of the conventional 
logistics regression to be kept43.
Ethical considerations
This study involved a secondary analysis of de_identified data from the PMA Ethiopia. The PMA Ethiopia 
survey was conducted strictly under the ethical rules and regulations of world health organization and IIRB of 
Ethiopian Health and Nutrition Research Institute (EHNRI). Informed consent was obtained from respondents 
during the data collection process of PMA Ethiopia during the entire data collection period from Oct 2019 
to Nov 2020 for the baseline survey and six week postpartum follow up interview. PMA surrey has been also 
conducted after obtained ethical approval from Bloomberg School of Public Health at Johns Hopkins University 
in Baltimore, USA. The data used for this study can be obtained upon request from PMA, the details are 
mentioned in elsewhere and the datasets used to produce estimates for this study were publicly available from 
the PMA website. https://www.pmadata.org/data/request-access-datas sets, the publicly available versions and 
accessed after submitting a concept note to the manuscript the data lab system, the online data set archive or 
repository.
Results
Magnitude of IPV during pregnancy as measured in the extended six weeks postpartum 
period
This study reported IPV experience among enrolled pregnant women during the index pregnancy as measured 
during the extended six weeks postpartum period.
The proportion of women who had reported experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV 
during the index pregnancy as measured in the extended 6 weeks postpartum was found to be 12.14% (95%CI: 
10.66%, 13.79%). A slightly higher percentage of women had reported that they have experienced at least of one 
form of sexual IPV 8.09% (95%CI: 6.91%, 9.44%) than experiencing at least one form of physical IPV 6.02% 
(95%CI: 4.94%, 7.31%) (Fig. 1).

Distribution IPV during the index pregnancy as measured six week postpartum by selected 
independent variables, merged panel and six week postpartum data sets
This study had reported IPV experience among enrolled pregnant women during the index pregnancy as 
measured during the extended six weeks postpartum period.
The proportion of women who had reported experiencing at least one form of IPV ranged from 9.29% among 
women aged 40 to 49 years old to 14.93% among those six week postpartum women aged 15 to 19 years. This 
same figure was 9.24% for the women in the well to do households to 11.18% of those dwelling in the poorest 
households. Similarly, 13.57% of rural residents and 14.29% of women living in Tigray region and 4.85% of 
residents of Addis Ababa had reported that they had experienced at least one form of IPV. Likewise, 12.89% 
of those with large family size and 11.73% of women with no formal education have reported that they have 
experienced at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV while one in 10 six week postpartum women who 
are followers orthodox religion have also reported IPV experience (Table 2).
In the same fashion, 14.28% of women who reported that their husband who had other wife and 11.58% of 
those who married more than once have reported experiencing IPV. Similarly, among women who reported 
that their husbands felt very happy for the index pregnancy 10.63% of them have experienced at least one form 
of physical and/or sexual IPV. Similarly, the proportion of women who have reported experiencing at least one 
form of IPV was 11.17% among those who had 1 to 2 child. This proportion was 12.00% among women who 
reported that they did not wanted to have another child by enrollment. Likewise 13.84% of never users and 
9.00% of those who reported that they have started using contraceptive by six weeks postpartum had reported 
experiencing at least one form of IPV respectively (Table 2).
Last but not least, 11.40% of those whose desired place of birth for most recent pregnancy was health facility 
and 11.89% those whose desired birth attendant was health professional reported that they have experienced at 
least one form of physical and sexual IPV(Table 2).
Factors affecting IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in the extended postpartum 
six weeks
This study had reported IPV experience among enrolled pregnant women during the index pregnancy as 
measured during the extended six weeks postpartum period.
The ICC of the intercept only or model null was found to be 41.0% which indicated high clustering of 
observation of IPV cases with EAs which in turn is not in agreement of the conventional logistics regression 
independent observation assumptions. Hence, guarantees the use of the multilevel statistical modeling which 
relaxes the independent observation assumption of the conventional logistics regression statistical modeling 
method. About model fitness the final model was found to be fitted; details for the intercept only model a 
loglikilihood of −742.194, AIC of 1488.387 and BIC of 1499.872 while the respective model fitness values have 
been reduced to −579.9988, 1205.998 and 1333.626 respectively in the final model, hence the final model was fit.
This study investigated factors contributing to women experience of at least one form of physical and/or 
sexual violence. Those women whose husband has other wives had higher likelihood of experiencing at least 
one form of physical and/or sexual IPV while those women who were residents of Afar region had lower odds 
of experiencing IPV.
The likelihood of experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index pregnancy as 
measured at six weeks postpartum was 2.14 (95%CI: 1.04, 4.38) times higher among women whose husband had 
other wives’ compared to those who did not have. On the contrary, women who were residents of Afar region 
had only 0.14 (95%CI: 0.03, 0.79) odds of experiencing one form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index 
pregnancy (Table 3).
Discussion
In the SDG era, the aim of this study was to determine the magnitude of intimate partner violence among 
pregnant women during their index pregnancy as measured at six weeks postpartum and identify its correlates 
using merged baseline and six weeks data from PMA cohort one longitudinal study on maternal and newborn 
health. Accordingly,  experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index pregnancy as 
measured in extended six weeks postpartum period was found to be 12.14% (95%CI: 10.66%, 13.79%). A slightly 
higher percentage of women reported that they have experienced at least of form of sexual IPV: 8.09% (95%CI: 
6.91%, 9.44%) than experiencing at least one form of physical IPV: 6.02% (95%CI: 4.94%, 7.31%).
Experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in 
the extended six weeks postpartum period was in line with9,16,44,45. It was lower than the pooled magnitude 
reported in different parts of Ethiopian and in East Africa12,20,46–49. This might be attributed to that two studies 
were based on demographic and health survey data which include emotion/physiological violence while this 
study entertains only physical and/or sexual IPV. Moreover, this study target currently pregnant women with the 
focus on IPV during the index pregnancy while other studies asked women about their experience during their 
pregnancy in the past years. In line with the finding from a studies16,44,47 sexual violence is higher than physical 
violence’s. The prevalence of IPV in line with findings from studies28,44,50.
Moreover, the unadjusted prevalence of IPV has shown statistically significant increase in the two years’ time 
from 2019 to 21. Over the two years; from Nov 2019 to Nov 2021 a statistically significant 4% change increase has 
been observed in the prevalence of IPV from 12.14% (95%CI: 10.66%, 13.79%) in 2019 to 16.7% (95%CI:14.81%, 
18.76%) in 202116 though the further analysis conducted using the 2021 survey16 does not include Tigary region 
since data were not collected in the region due to the conflict erupted. This signifies that the public importance 
of IPV has been increased in Ethiopia which is one policy implication to strengthen the combat against all forms 
of IPV among women and girls so as to be closer to the 2030 SDG targets of 5.2.1 and 16.239.

The finding that experiencing IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in the six weeks postpartum 
showed regional variation might be related with the varying degree of birth preparedness and complication 
readiness activities across regions51 and better implementation of the recent health sector transformation 
plan52 in general and the reproductive health policy running 2021 to 25 in particular2. In addition, acceptance 
of violence and women beating by women and the community across the country might have explained the 
regional variation in IPV experience17–19,53–55. A study56 stressed on the influence of the community towards 
IPV by asserting that there is still a need for further work focused particularly on the root causes of aggression 
towards women at the household, group and community levels.
The finding that women whose husband has other wives had an increased odds of experiencing IPV in the 
extended six weeks postpartum period is likely to be related with male dominance in deciding the number of 
children that the family would possess along with the timing, since, women are living in a society where male 
dominance is socially and culturally accepted57–59. The effect of male dominance can be extended to halting 
immediate postpartum women contraceptive use decision, resulting unintended pregnancy and women being 
unhappy when learned their pregnancy60,61 which might increase the odds of IPV.
Couple sociodemographic characteristics were not found significant in this study while previous studies 
reported a finding like this study and an association report with IPV as well. Like studies12,62,63 age of the 
respondent is not found significant while studies9,20,47,48,54,62–67 had reported that advanced respondent age 
and lower to middle wealth index were found to increase the odds of IPV. In line with studies44,46 respondent 
educational status is not found significantly affecting IPV, while studies12,20,34,64 reported that no formal 
education was found to increase the odds of IPV. In this study husband educational status and age does not 
show significant association with IPV while studies14,28 reported that husband better educational status lowered 
the odds of IPV and other studies20,46,64 reported that no or primary husband educational attainment increased 
the odds of IPV. Like a study68 place of residence is not significant in this study and whereas studies34,63 have 
reported that rural residence is associated with an increased odds of IPV. In line with studies34,63 couples age 
difference is not significant in this study.
The above observed discrepancies might be related with difference in study design as this study is longitudinal 
while others were merely cross sectional; nature of the study population: in this study only currently pregnant 
women were asked about whether they encountered physical or sexual IPV during their index pregnancy using 
10 items while other studies consider women who gave birth in the past years too; scope of the study and how 
the outcome variable was measured, this study used 10 items to measure physical and/or sexual violence while 
other studies use different set of questions and include physiological/emotional violence14,20,47,66. For a number 
of studies28,51,65 the study setting is different, were conducted in a clinical setting.
This study was not spared from limitations. variables such as respondent and husband alcohol or substance 
use, childhood experience, media exposure, family and community support towards IPV prevention during 
pregnancy and postpartum period, household decision making etc. were missing. In addition, though self-
reported, it minimized the recall bias given the six week follow up survey asked women their IPV experience 
during their index pregnancy while other studies including studies further analyzed Demographic Health 
Surveys asked women who delivered in the past years and who were pregnant by the time of the survey which 
introduced a more recall bias lead to inflation of the finding given they may have multiple birth over the past 
years since the study population in such studies is heterogeneous.
As a strength, this study measured IPV during the index pregnancy by the extended six weeks postpartum 
periods for a cohort of women followed form one month to 12–13 months, half of the entire follow up. In 
addition, though self-reported, it minimized recall bias given the six week follow up survey asked IPV experience

Conclusion
Experiencing at least one form of physical and/or sexual IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in the 
extended six weeks postpartum period was found to be 12.14%. A slightly higher percentage of women reported 
that they have experienced at least one of form of sexual IPV 8.09% (95%CI: 6.91%, 9.44%) than experiencing at 
least one form of physical IPV 6.02% (95%CI: 4.94%, 7.31%).
The overall burden of IPV during the index pregnancy as measured in the extended six weeks postpartum 
period was considerably high. More work needed to be done to achieve zero tolerance against any form of 
violence against women and girls in general and IPV among pregnant women in particular. Activities and efforts 
which are specific to regions and that address the problem of polygamy are hoped to address the problem IPV. 
Efforts targeted in counseling women about how to prevent IPV during their ANC and postnatal visits along 
with advising them the use of inter pregnancy contraception and empowering them to decide on their fertility 
desire and use of reproductive health services are found imperative to reduce the odds of IPV among pregnant

women. Encouraging women to plan and space their pregnancy were found imperative to combat the growing 
burden of IPV. Such activities should be tailored along the maternal and new born care continuum.
Future PMA and similar surveys need to consider collecting data on potential confounder such as alcohol 
or substance abuse, childhood IPV experience, husband and community support with regard to IPV. Moreover, 
there is a need for future similar surveys to collect information on the emotional aspect of intimate partner 
violence in particular and domestic violence in general. The authors are planning consider facility level factors by 
merging PMA service facility data with women and household data to consider the effect of facility side factors.
Policy and practical implication of findings
The implication of the findings calls key actors and the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia Health Minster 
to design and implement region specific interventions and programs which targeted women in polygamous 
marriage to avert the pronounced IPV problem among pregnant women. Such activities should be tailored along 
with the maternal and new born care continuum. Moreover, creating institutional capacity in the health system 
through strengthening and expanding one stop centers to provide medical treatment, care, and psychosocial 
support and support for victims and survivors can be considered as imperative and was implied. In addition, the 
finding gave an insight that installing rapid referral system and linkage to the legal system is vital. Furthermore, 
working on early marriage and counseling on childbirth; and spaced pregnancies for those young couples could 
be critical to avert the growing burden of IPV. Further implication of this study is installing contraceptive and 
violence related preconception care packages in the health system which is very critical in the combat against 
IPV and any form of gender based violence. Finally, determining the prevalence of violence could serve as one 
of the zero tolerance indicators to monitor the progress towards SDG 5.2.1 and any strategy and policy changes 
needed in light of the observed progress. Most importantly, involving male in the combat against this growing 
burden of IPV is implied as strategic policy implication69.
